intro:
These exercises take the chapter's central claim apart and rebuild it from the bottom: an async function in Rust produces an inert value, and nothing runs until an executor polls that value to completion. The warm-up and code-reading tasks make you say out loud what poll, Poll::Pending, and the executor/reactor split actually do; the implementation tasks have you hand-write the state machine the compiler normally writes for you, so the poll-by-poll mechanics stop being mysterious. By the time you have written a future that yields N times and composed two awaits in one async fn, the enum-shaped state machine model is no longer a metaphor — it is the thing you typed.

The debugging and design exercises then push the model into the situations where it earns its keep: a future that never yields (and therefore wedges the executor), and a real request that fans out to several outbound calls and must be cancelled on a deadline. The through-line is that suspension makes ownership, task lifetime, and cancellation visible in your types. Cancel means drop the future; locals held across an .await become fields of the future; cleanup of partially acquired state is the author's job, not the runtime's. Get those three right and the rest of async Rust is consequence.

exerciseSolutions.title: Explain what calling an async fn actually does
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Calling build_label("billing", "/ready") does not start the work. The call expression evaluates to a value of an opaque future type — the compiler-generated state machine for build_label — and that value is inert. None of the function body has run: no YieldOnce has been constructed, no .await has fired, no String has been formatted. The chapter's one-line summary applies exactly here: calling an async function produces a value and starts nothing.

The only thing that ever advances the future is a call to its poll method, and the component that calls poll is the executor. In this listing the executor is block_on. It pins the future with Box::pin, builds a Context from a Waker, and then loops, calling future.as_mut().poll(&mut cx). Each iteration the future runs forward until it either suspends or finishes.

When poll returns Poll::Pending, no OS thread is blocked. Pending is the future's way of handing control back to the executor and saying "I cannot make progress right now." The executor is then free to do other work — in a real runtime, poll a different ready task. Here block_on simply prints poll = pending and loops again. Crucially, the thread is never parked inside the future's body waiting on a socket; the suspension point is a return out of poll, not a blocking syscall. That is the whole efficiency argument for async: one thread can service many suspended futures because suspension is a return, not a block.

A full runtime splits into two cooperating roles. The executor is the scheduler that decides which ready task to poll next. The reactor (the IO driver) watches the operating system for readiness — a socket becoming readable, a timer firing — and signals the corresponding waker so the executor knows to poll that task again. In this std-only example there is no real IO, so there is no reactor; the NoopWake waker does nothing and block_on just re-polls in a tight loop. block_on is standing in for the executor role: it is the part that turns the future's description into actual progress by repeatedly calling poll.
criteria: States that build_label("billing", "/ready") constructs an opaque future value and runs none of the body — no YieldOnce, no .await, no format! yet.
Identifies poll as the only advancing operation and block_on (the executor) as the caller of poll in this listing.
Explains that Poll::Pending returns control to the executor instead of parking a thread, since suspension is a return out of poll.
Distinguishes executor (scheduler) from reactor (IO readiness) and names block_on as the executor here, with no reactor present in the std-only example.

exerciseSolutions.title: Trace the Handshake state machine by hand
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Construct the Handshake from Example 2 with stage = Stage::Start and remaining_polls = 1, then trace the driver loop poll by poll. The match arms are ordered, and the guarded arm Stage::Waiting if self.remaining_polls > 0 fires before the plain Stage::Waiting arm, so order matters.

Poll #1: stage is Start. The Start arm sets stage = Waiting and returns Poll::Pending. State after: stage = Waiting, remaining_polls = 1. The driver prints "pending stage = Waiting" and "pending retries = 1".

Poll #2: stage is Waiting and remaining_polls (1) > 0, so the guarded arm fires: it decrements remaining_polls to 0 and returns Poll::Pending. State after: stage = Waiting, remaining_polls = 0. The driver prints "pending stage = Waiting" and "pending retries = 0".

Poll #3: stage is Waiting but remaining_polls (0) is not > 0, so the guard fails and the plain Stage::Waiting arm fires: it sets stage = Done and returns Poll::Ready("connected"). The driver prints "ready = connected" and breaks.

So poll is called three times before Poll::Ready is produced — two Pending results then one Ready. The sequence of (stage at entry, result) is: (Start, Pending), (Waiting, Pending), (Waiting, Ready).

remaining_polls is the retry budget: it is the number of extra Pending trips the future stays in the Waiting stage after the initial Start-to-Waiting transition. While the counter is above zero each poll decrements it and yields Pending; when it reaches zero the next poll falls through to the unguarded Waiting arm, transitions to Done, and reports Ready. On each Pending the driver loop prints the current stage and the remaining retry count, which is exactly what lets you watch the machine advance: every Pending either changed the stage (Start to Waiting) or lowered remaining_polls (1 to 0), so progress is guaranteed and the loop terminates.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Hand trace: three polls, two Pending, then Ready; the guarded Waiting arm fires before the plain one.
criteria: Trace shows Start returning Pending, then Waiting (remaining_polls 1) returning Pending, then Waiting returning Ready, in that order.
States poll is called three times before Poll::Ready is returned.
Explains remaining_polls is the retry budget keeping the future in Waiting/Pending until it hits zero.
Notes each Pending prints the current stage and the remaining retries from the driver loop.

exerciseSolutions.title: Write a future that yields N times before completing
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Generalize YieldOnce — which flips a single bool — into CountdownYield, which counts an integer down. The struct holds a single field, remaining, recording how many Pending results are still owed. The poll signature is fixed by the exercise: fn poll(self: Pin<&mut Self>, cx: &mut Context<'_>) -> Poll<&'static str>.

The logic in poll is: if remaining > 0, decrement it and return Poll::Pending; otherwise return Poll::Ready("done"). For n = 3 this returns Pending on the first three polls (remaining going 3 to 2 to 1 to 0) and Ready on the fourth poll, which is exactly three Pending results before completion.

The receiver self: Pin<&mut Self> matters here. To mutate remaining you go through self, the pinned mutable reference — not a separate owned copy of the struct. Because the fields of CountdownYield are plain integers and the type contains no self-referential borrow, the type is Unpin, so you can freely assign self.remaining -= 1 through the pinned reference (this is what `mut self: Pin<&mut Self>` plus auto-deref gives you). The mutation persists across polls precisely because it writes back into the pinned future the executor owns, not into a temporary. Drive it with the chapter's block_on loop and you will see three poll = pending lines, then label = done.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: CountdownYield reports Pending n times (here 3) then Ready("done"), mutating its counter through the pinned receiver.
criteria: poll signature is exactly fn poll(self: Pin<&mut Self>, cx: &mut Context<'_>) -> Poll<&'static str> (written with `mut self` so the receiver is mutable).
For n = 3 the future returns Poll::Pending three times and then Poll::Ready("done").
The counter is mutated via self.remaining through the Pin<&mut Self> receiver, not an owned copy.
Driver output shows exactly three poll = pending lines before the ready value, confirmed by the inline expected output.

exerciseSolutions.title: Compose two awaits inside one async fn
exerciseSolutions.solution:
connect_then_call awaits two YieldOnce subfutures in sequence and then formats the result. The body is: let _ = YieldOnce::new(service).await; let _ = YieldOnce::new(route).await; format!("{}:{}", service, route). The two awaits run one after the other — the second YieldOnce is not even constructed until the first has resolved to Ready.

Each YieldOnce yields exactly one Poll::Pending before becoming Ready, so two of them in sequence produce two Pending results total. Under the chapter's block_on you therefore see two poll = pending lines, then connected = billing:/ready. This is additive precisely because the awaits are sequential, not concurrent: the combined future is suspended once for the first subfuture and once for the second.

The locals service and route must survive across both await points because the final format! uses them after the second suspension. In the compiler's lowering, this is not a runtime accident — it is structural. The async fn becomes one enum-shaped state machine, and any local whose value is needed after an .await is stored as a field of that future so it lives as long as the future does. service and route are needed after both suspensions, so they become fields. This is the same mechanism that, later in real code, turns a borrow held across an .await into a lifetime that lasts the whole future.

Relate this to the chapter's model: each .await becomes a distinct variant of the generated state machine. There is roughly a variant for "about to start," a variant for "suspended at the first YieldOnce" (holding service and route), a variant for "suspended at the second YieldOnce" (still holding service and route), and a terminal variant. poll is a match that advances from one variant to the next, returning Pending at each suspension. The hand-written Handshake in Example 2 is exactly this shape spelled out by hand — explicit states, explicit pending, explicit ready — and connect_then_call is the version the compiler writes for you.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Two sequential awaits produce two Pending results; service and route survive both suspensions as fields of the generated future.
criteria: connect_then_call awaits both YieldOnce values in order and returns the formatted "billing:/ready" String.
Predicts two Pending prints, one per sequential YieldOnce, shown in the inline expected output.
Explains the awaited locals service and route become fields of the generated future and must outlive each suspension.
Connects each .await to a distinct variant of the compiler-generated state machine, tying it to Example 2's hand-written shape.

exerciseSolutions.title: Fix a manual future that never yields
exerciseSolutions.solution:
There are two defects, and they are opposite failures of the same rule: every Pending must change the future's own state so progress is guaranteed and termination is reachable.

Defect one is the early-Ready arm. The Start arm returns Poll::Ready immediately instead of transitioning to a Waiting stage and returning Pending. This defeats the purpose of the future entirely: it never suspends, so it models no waiting at all. The whole point of a future is to be able to report "not yet" and hand control back; an immediate Ready is just a synchronous function in disguise.

Defect two is the non-advancing Pending arm. A Waiting arm returns Poll::Pending without changing the stage and without decrementing any counter. This is the classic infinite-loop bug: the future returns Pending, the executor polls it again, it is in exactly the same state, so it returns Pending again, forever. block_on would spin without end because the future never changes anything between polls — there is no path to Ready. (In a real runtime it would be even worse: a future that returns Pending without arranging for its waker to fire can hang silently.)

The fix is to make every Pending advance the state. Rewrite the transitions so Start moves to Waiting and yields Pending; Waiting decrements a retry counter and yields Pending while the budget remains; and when the budget is exhausted Waiting moves to Done and returns Ready. Now each poll strictly advances either the stage or the counter, so the future returns Poll::Ready after a finite, predictable number of polls (one for Start, remaining_polls more for the countdown, then the final transition). Tracing it under the driver loop confirms termination: every iteration the printed stage or retry count is different from the last, which is the visible signature of guaranteed progress. This is exactly the invariant Example 2 maintains — every Pending either changes the Stage or lowers remaining_polls.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Both defects fixed: Start now yields instead of completing early, and the Waiting arm decrements its budget so every Pending advances state.
criteria: Diagnosis names the early-Ready Start arm and the non-advancing Pending Waiting arm as the two defects.
Fixed poll advances Stage or decrements remaining_polls on every Pending, guaranteeing progress.
Fixed future returns Poll::Ready after a finite, predictable number of polls (three for this construction).
Explanation ties the infinite loop to a future returning Pending without changing its own state, contrasting with Example 2's invariant.

exerciseSolutions.title: Design a cancellable fan-out for one request
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The request handler parses input, fans out to several outbound RPCs, joins their results, and writes to a database, all under a single overall timeout. The design splits cleanly along the ownership question the runtime forces you to answer.

What stays borrowed versus what must be owned. Values used only inside the handler's own stack frame — the parsed request struct that you read fields from sequentially, a &str slice you only inspect — can stay borrowed, because they never leave the parent's scope. But anything a spawned child task captures must be owned (or '\''static-shared) before the task is spawned. A child task may be moved onto another worker thread and may outlive the exact stack frame that created it, so it cannot hold a plain borrow into the parent's locals. Concretely: if each outbound RPC needs the request id and a target endpoint, clone or move owned copies (String, an Arc of shared config, an owned endpoint) into each child. The discriminator is not "is it cheap to copy" but "does it cross the spawn boundary." If you do not spawn detached tasks and instead keep the children as futures joined in place (join!/a join-set the parent awaits), borrows can survive, because the children never escape the parent future's scope and the borrow checker can see that the parent outlives them.

What cancelling a child actually means. In async Rust a future only advances when it is polled, so cancelling a child means dropping its future — the parent simply stops polling it. There is no signal delivered into the middle of the child and no thread to interrupt; you destroy the state machine and its in-progress work stops at its last suspension point. So the parent triggers cancellation by dropping the child futures (or by dropping the join-set / select! losers), not by calling any cancel() method on the child.

The structured-concurrency rule. The parent owns the entire fan-out and the children cannot outlive it. Implement the timeout as a select between the joined fan-out and a timer: if the timer wins, the parent returns and the joined fan-out future is dropped, which drops every still-pending child. Because the children are owned by the parent's future (not spawned detached), dropping the parent drops them — there are no orphans continuing to run after the request is over. The parent also surfaces the first failure: if one RPC errors, the join can short-circuit and the remaining children are dropped (cancelled) the same way. This is the join-set / request-scoped task-group / parent-owned cancellation-token pattern; the runtime API varies but the ownership rule does not.

Cleanup of partially acquired state. Dropping a future stops it at its last await point, but drop alone does not unwind business-level state. If a child had already, say, taken a distributed lock, written a tentative row, or reserved a quota before it was dropped, that partially acquired state is not rolled back automatically. Cancellation safety has to be designed into the future itself: hold resources in RAII guards whose Drop releases them, defer irreversible side effects until after the last await so a drop before that point leaves nothing to undo, or structure the operation so an interrupted attempt is idempotent or explicitly compensated. The chapter's correction is the load-bearing point: cancel usually means drop the future, and if the future must clean up partially acquired state, that cleanup must be explicit in the future's own design.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Parent-owned fan-out under a timeout: borrowed-locally vs owned-before-spawn, cancel = drop the future, cleanup must be explicit.
criteria: Separates values borrowed only within the parent scope from values that must be owned before a task crosses the spawn boundary.
States that cancelling a child means dropping its future — the parent stops polling it — with no signal or thread interrupt.
Asserts the parent owns the fan-out so children cannot outlive it, and surfaces the first failure via short-circuiting join.
Notes that cleanup of partially acquired state must be explicit in the future's own design (Drop guards, deferred side effects), since drop alone does not unwind it.

labSolution.expectedOutput:
poll = pending
poll = pending
result = session-open
pending count = 2
labSolution.explanation:
The Handshake future is a hand-written state machine over three Stage values: Connect, Authenticate, Ready. The poll method advances exactly one stage per call. On the first poll it is in Connect, so it moves the stage to Authenticate and returns Poll::Pending. On the second poll it is in Authenticate, so it moves the stage to Ready and returns Poll::Pending again. On the third poll it is in Ready, the terminal stage, so it returns Poll::Ready("session-open"). Each Pending strictly advances the stage, which is what guarantees the future terminates rather than spinning.

The block_on driver supplies the executor role. It pins the future with Box::pin, builds a Context from a no-op Waker, and loops calling poll. Every time poll returns Poll::Pending it increments a pending counter and prints "poll = pending"; when poll returns Poll::Ready it returns the value together with the pending count. Because the future yields Pending on the Connect and Authenticate stages, block_on prints "poll = pending" twice and the counter ends at 2.

Main constructs the Handshake at Stage::Connect, runs it to completion under block_on, and binds (result, pending_count) = ("session-open", 2). It then prints "result = session-open" and "pending count = 2". The four output lines — two pending prints, the result, and the pending count — are exactly the expected output. The polls field is incremented each poll for instrumentation but is not part of the printed output here.

reviewAnswers.question: Why does calling an async fn in Rust start no work, and what type does the call expression produce?
reviewAnswers.answer: Calling an async fn produces a value and runs none of the function body — async functions are lazy. The call expression evaluates to an opaque, compiler-generated type that implements the Future trait (the function's state machine), and that value is inert until something polls it. Work begins only when an executor calls Future::poll on it; before the first poll, no locals have been initialized and no .await has run. This laziness is the foundation of the whole model: execution and thread placement are decisions the executor makes, not side effects of the call.

reviewAnswers.question: What does the compiler build from an async function, and what determines which locals become fields of that state machine?
reviewAnswers.answer: The compiler rewrites the async fn into one enum-shaped state machine where each .await is a suspension point, modeled as a variant, and poll is a match that advances from one variant to the next. The locals that become fields of that state machine are exactly those whose values must survive across an .await — that is, any local still needed after a suspension point. Locals used only between two awaits and never read afterward do not need to be stored, while a value (or a borrow) held across an await is kept alive as a field for as long as the future lives. This is why borrows held across awaits turn into lifetimes that last the whole future, and why captured state must outlive each suspension.

reviewAnswers.question: Why does Future::poll take a Pin<&mut Self> receiver rather than a plain &mut Self?
reviewAnswers.answer: Because the generated state machine can be self-referential: a local borrowed across an .await becomes a field that holds a pointer into another field of the same future. Moving such a value in memory would leave that internal pointer dangling, corrupting the future. Pin<&mut Self> is the type-level guarantee that the future will not be moved after polling begins, so those internal references stay valid. Many ordinary futures are movable and implement Unpin, but the poll signature must remain strong enough to handle the general self-referential case at the runtime boundary.

reviewAnswers.question: What are the two cooperating parts of an async runtime, and what does each one do?
reviewAnswers.answer: An async runtime is an executor plus a reactor. The executor is the scheduler: it owns the set of tasks and decides which ready task to poll next, driving futures forward by calling poll. The reactor (the IO driver) watches the operating system for readiness events — a socket becoming readable, a timer firing — and when an event arrives it signals the corresponding task's waker so the executor knows to poll that task again. A future returns Poll::Pending and registers its waker; the reactor later wakes it; the executor re-polls. In the chapter's std-only examples there is no real IO, so block_on plays the executor role and the no-op waker stands in for the reactor.

reviewAnswers.question: In async Rust, what does cancelling a future mean operationally, and what is the future author still responsible for?
reviewAnswers.answer: A future only advances when it is polled, so cancelling it operationally means dropping it: the owner stops polling and destroys the state machine, which halts its in-progress work at its last suspension point. This is what a timeout, a select! that picks another branch, or a dropped join-set does — there is no signal delivered into the future and no thread to interrupt. The author is still responsible for cleanup of any partially acquired state: dropping the future does not unwind business-level effects like a held lock, a tentative write, or a reserved quota. Cancellation safety must be designed into the future itself, typically via RAII Drop guards that release resources and by deferring irreversible side effects until after the last await.
